meta.title: Cholera Tracker: Global
meta.description: Independent, sourced tracker of cholera worldwide in 2026: WHO case and death counts, countries reporting cases, how this year compares with 2025, WHO's risk level and a dated timeline.
meta.disclaimer: This tracker summarises WHO, ECDC, UNICEF and national health authority reports and named news outlets. Reported figures include suspected cases and understate the true burden. It is not medical or travel advice. If someone has sudden, severe watery diarrhoea, seek medical care straight away.

headline: WHO counts 275,284 cases and 2,601 deaths in 28 countries by 30 August, 43% fewer cases than a year earlier. 2025 had the most deaths since 1999.

status.label: Slowing · below 2025's pace
status.summary: WHO counted 275,284 cholera and acute watery diarrhoea cases and 2,601 deaths in 28 countries from 1 January to 30 August, 43% fewer cases and 58% fewer deaths than a year earlier, and August's cases fell 25% from July. Afghanistan, Nigeria and DR Congo report the most cases. WHO rated the global risk very high in June, and 2025 brought the most cholera deaths reported to WHO since 1999.

regions.note: Latest sourced 2026 total for each country; dates vary. Nigeria and DR Congo are from WHO's August update (to 30 Aug) and Afghanistan from WHO's country office (to end of August); the rest are from ECDC's monthly overview (date in each note). WHO counts 28 countries with cases this year: pale shading marks countries with cases but no total tracked here, and other countries aren't tracked here.

claims.claim: Cholera is a disease of the past
claims.detail: 47 countries reported 451,499 cases and 7,870 deaths to WHO in 2025, the most deaths since 1999. 28 countries reported cases in the first eight months of 2026.

claims.claim: Reported cholera cases are higher in 2026 than in 2025
claims.detail: WHO counts 43% fewer cases and 58% fewer deaths from 1 January to 30 August 2026 than in the same months of 2025. Large outbreaks continue in Afghanistan, Nigeria and DR Congo.

claims.claim: Official counts capture every cholera case
claims.detail: WHO says its figures reflect surveillance reports, not the actual burden, which is estimated to be substantially higher because many cases go unreported.

claims.claim: Antibiotics are the main treatment for cholera
claims.detail: Most patients recover with prompt oral rehydration solution, which replaces lost fluids and salts. WHO advises antibiotics for severely ill patients, alongside intravenous fluids, and does not recommend mass antibiotic use.

claims.claim: A handful of countries account for most cholera cases and deaths
claims.detail: WHO says seven countries (Angola, Bangladesh, DR Congo, Nigeria, South Sudan, Sudan and Yemen) accounted for about 90% of the cases and deaths reported in 2025.

positions.text: 212,857 cases, including 1,943 deaths, reported worldwide since 1 January. Nigeria reported the most new cases and deaths in the past month.
Cholera is spreading across borders in West and Central Africa; urgent action is needed to protect millions of children.

timeline.title: WHO's global cholera reports become monthly updates
timeline.body: After 32 external situation reports, WHO's reports on the multi-country cholera situation continue in 2026 as monthly epidemiological updates.

timeline.title: WHO: 79,740 cases and 1,010 deaths by late April
timeline.body: WHO's monthly update counts cholera and acute watery diarrhoea cases in 22 countries from 1 January to 26 April. April's 20,100 new cases were 20% more than March's.

timeline.title: WHO: May cases up 43%; global risk very high
timeline.body: WHO counts 114,829 cases and 1,318 deaths in 23 countries from 1 January to 31 May, including 29,610 new cases in May. It rates the global risk very high, with about 1 billion people at risk.

timeline.title: UNICEF: cholera is spreading across borders in West and Central Africa
timeline.body: UNICEF says outbreaks are accelerating in six countries: DR Congo, the Republic of the Congo, Nigeria, Chad, Cameroon and the Central African Republic. It reports more than 50,000 cases and 338 deaths in Nigeria this year, and more than 30,400 cases and nearly 700 deaths in DR Congo. The same strain is circulating in Chad, Cameroon and Nigeria around Lake Chad. UNICEF asks for $15 million for the next six months.

timeline.title: ECDC: 212,857 cases worldwide this year
timeline.body: ECDC's monthly overview counts 212,857 cases, including 1,943 deaths, since 1 January. Nigeria reported the most new cases (41,296) and deaths (242) in the month to 26 August.

timeline.title: Afghanistan's acute watery diarrhoea cases fall in August
timeline.body: WHO reports 18,329 cases of acute watery diarrhoea with dehydration and 4 deaths in August, 23.6% fewer cases than July's 23,985. Afghanistan has recorded 102,469 such cases this year.

timeline.title: WHO: 2025 had the most cholera deaths since 1999
timeline.body: 47 countries reported 451,499 cases and 7,870 deaths to WHO in 2025. Deaths rose 30% although fewer cases were reported, and seven countries accounted for about 90% of cases and deaths. WHO says the true burden is substantially higher.

timeline.title: WHO: 275,284 cases and 2,601 deaths in 28 countries
timeline.body: WHO's August update, now published in its Weekly Epidemiological Record, covers 1 January to 30 August: 43% fewer cases and 58% fewer deaths than a year earlier. August's 41,915 new cases were 25% fewer than July's. Nigeria (69,263) and DR Congo (44,773) report the most cases in Africa.

timeline.title: ECDC: 249,136 cases worldwide this year
timeline.body: ECDC's monthly overview counts 249,136 cases, including 1,970 deaths, from 1 January to 28 September, against 436,268 cases and 4,449 deaths at the same point in 2025. In the month to 28 September it recorded 46,153 new cases and 140 deaths; Afghanistan (34,378), DR Congo (8,505) and Yemen (1,885) reported the most cases. ECDC's totals are a separate count from the WHO figures above.

history.text: WHO issues regular external situation reports on the multi-country cholera outbreak; the sixth comes out in September.
47 countries report 451,499 cases and 7,870 deaths to WHO, the highest death toll since 1999. Seven countries account for about 90%.
WHO's reports become monthly epidemiological updates in January and move into its Weekly Epidemiological Record in July. By 30 August, 28 countries report 275,284 cases and 2,601 deaths.

facts.a: Through food or water contaminated with the faeces of an infected person. It spreads where safe water and sanitation are lacking; WHO links recent surges to conflict, climate change and inequality.

Sudden, profuse watery diarrhoea, sometimes with vomiting, which can cause severe dehydration within hours. Most infected people have mild or no symptoms. Symptoms usually begin 12 hours to 5 days after infection.

Most people recover with prompt oral rehydration solution, which replaces lost fluids and salts. Severely dehydrated patients need intravenous fluids and antibiotics. Untreated, severe cholera can kill within hours.
Yes. Oral cholera vaccines are used in outbreaks and in high-risk areas, alongside safe water and sanitation, which WHO calls critical to preventing cholera.

facts.q: Why do the counts include acute watery diarrhoea?
facts.a: Many countries report suspected cases without testing each one, and some, such as Afghanistan, report acute watery diarrhoea with dehydration. WHO's monthly figures combine cholera and acute watery diarrhoea, and WHO says reported numbers understate the true burden.
